title: Zero-Flow Encoders
claim: A flow trained between identical distributions vanishes everywhere at the midpoint time, even though it is nonzero before and after.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, time titles above, vector fields
description: Three square panels sit side by side, titled t=0.25, t=0.5 and t=0.75. Each panel shows a 2-D grid of small red arrows, the learned rectified-flow velocity field. The left panel also has blue scatter points forming a two-cluster Gaussian mixture, one cluster at upper right and one at lower left. At t=0.25 the red arrows are clearly visible and point in varied directions around the clusters. In the middle panel, at t=0.5, the arrows shrink to near-invisible dots, so the field looks almost empty apart from a few small arrows at the bottom-right corner. At t=0.75 the arrows are large and swirl in a pattern like the first panel. The eye goes first to the blue clusters, then to the blank middle panel.
caption: "Zero-flow" phenomenon. Rectified flow trained on identical distributions (a Gaussian mixture, blue points) with independent coupling. At $t=0.5$, the flow becomes stationary almost everywhere. An explanation of this phenomenon can be found in Section [ref], and additional visualizations can be found in Figure [ref].
abstract: Flow-based methods have achieved significant success in various generative modeling tasks, capturing nuanced details within complex data distributions. However, few existing works have exploited this unique capability to resolve fine-grained structural details beyond generation tasks. This paper presents a flow-inspired framework for representation learning. First, we demonstrate that a rectified flow trained using independent coupling is zero everywhere at $t=0.5$ if and only if the source and target distributions are identical. We term this property the \emph{zero-flow criterion}. Second, we show that this criterion can certify conditional independence, thereby extracting \emph{sufficient information} from the data. Third, we translate this criterion into a tractable, simulation-free loss function that enables learning amortized Markov blankets in graphical models and latent representations in self-supervised learning tasks. Experiments on both simulated and real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach. The code reproducing our experiments can be found at: https://github.com/probabilityFLOW/zfe.
